content: The study identified 79 eligible guidelines, while 1,753 were excluded based on their titles and abstracts. An additional 54 papers were excluded due to duplication or ineligibility. Among the guidelines, 9 were related to antenatal care (ANC), and 15 ANC guidelines were selected for review. Additionally, 70 guidelines addressing specific situations were included. Reference checking and expert identification contributed three additional guidelines each. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience were supported by an evidence base, including search strategies for qualitative meta-synthesis of women’s views. The inclusion criteria for studies required qualitative designs such as ethnography, phenomenology, case studies, grounded theory, and mixed methods. Data collection methods included interviews, focus group discussions, open-ended survey questions, diaries, and other narrative-based approaches. Studies needed to focus on women’s views, attitudes, experiences, facilitators, and barriers related to routine ANC, excluding those addressing care in specific health or social conditions like HIV or malaria. The population of interest included pregnant or postnatal women, with studies published between January 2000 and August 2014 to capture experiences since the introduction of focused antenatal care (FANC) programs. No language restrictions were imposed, and non-English studies were translated when possible. Search terms targeted participants (e.g., women, patients, service users), areas of interest (e.g., antenatal care, maternal health services), and study designs (e.g., qualitative, ethnography, phenomenology). The search strategy was adapted for each database, including title, abstract, and keyword searches. Two independent reviewers screened studies at each stage, resolving disagreements through consensus or adjudication by a third reviewer. Reference lists and key authors were scrutinized, and back-chaining and forward-checking were conducted to identify additional relevant studies. Quality checks and inclusion/exclusion criteria were applied consistently. For healthcare providers’ views, qualitative studies using similar designs and data collection methods were included. These studies focused on staff experiences and views related to routine ANC provision, excluding those addressing specialist services for high-risk pregnancies. The population included staff in primary, secondary, and tertiary care settings, fulfilling the WHO definition of skilled birth attendants or identified as such by study authors. Auxiliary and lay health workers were included if they were paid to provide ANC. Studies were published between January 2000 and August 2014, with no language restrictions. The search strategy for indirect evidence on health systems interventions addressed three priority questions: the recommendation of group ANC as an alternative to standard ANC, interventions to communicate with and support pregnant women and their communities, and whether pregnant women should carry their own ANC case notes. Indirect evidence was considered if included in systematic reviews published within the last five years, relevant to ANC guideline questions, and addressing agreed-upon outcomes. Searches were conducted in databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, and grey literature sources like ministry of health documents and organizational websites. Interviews with stakeholders supplemented the literature review, particularly for cases with limited adoption or unsuccessful implementation of the WHO FANC model. Interviews were conducted in English or the primary language of the country, with notes taken during discussions. The interviews explored gaps in knowledge and participants’ experiences with the FANC model. Country case descriptions included profiles of mortality, resource availability, ANC coverage, and other indicators, with data compiled from WHO, World Bank, and other public datasets. The technical team also considered indirect evidence for health systems interventions, focusing on group ANC, communication strategies, and patient-held case notes. Systematic reviews published within the last five years were screened for relevance, and findings were summarized and discussed within the team. The evidence informed WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience.
